title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 283
paragraphs: The nature of the crocodile is as follows. During the four most wintry months this creature eats nothing. It has four feet and is an animal belonging both to land and water; for it produces and hatches its eggs on land, and the greater part of the day it remains upon dry land, but the whole of the night in the river — for the water in truth is warmer than the unclouded open air and the dew. Of all the mortal creatures we know, this one grows to the greatest bulk from the smallest beginning; for the eggs it produces are not much larger than those of geese, and the newly hatched young is in proportion to the egg, but as he grows he becomes as much as seventeen cubits long, and sometimes even larger. He has eyes like those of a pig and large tusky teeth in proportion to the size of his body; but unlike all other beasts he grows no tongue, nor does he move his lower jaw — he brings the upper jaw down towards the lower, being in this too unlike all other beasts. He has strong claws and a scaly hide upon his back which cannot be pierced. He is blind in the water, but in the air he is of very keen sight. Since he lives in the water, he keeps his mouth full of leeches; and whereas all other birds and beasts flee from him, the trochilus is a creature that is at peace with him, since from her he receives benefit. For the crocodile, having come out of the water onto the land and then having opened his mouth (which he is accustomed to do generally towards the West Wind), the trochilus then enters his mouth and swallows down the leeches; and the crocodile, being benefited, is pleased and does no harm to the trochilus.
